note: Both songs are built on a long list of Ganapati's food offerings (fruits, appam, sugarcane, dal, sesame, puffed rice, tender coconut). In 2 the list is the god's own table; in 4 it is what the worshipper sets before him with sit-ups and ear-holding.
audit_text_issue: 2 has a corrupt glyph in தன஧முலம்; 4 in செற஧முளை.

note: Both set the Lord against Death's messengers at the hour of death. Tirumular says those who think of the Lord will not be harmed by them; 8 is the prayer of one who has not done the thinking and asks Murugan to come anyway, on the peacock, at that moment.

The Kural says the heart melts at the thought of begging; 15 confesses the act, a poet praising patrons as Tamil's refuge 'with a wounded heart', and asks to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet.
Both describe women who want a man for his wealth and whose sweet invitations harm him; the Kural warns, 19 confesses to having trusted them.
Both make Murugan Siva's teacher: in 6 he teaches what precedes the Veda, in 12 he punishes Brahma and gives the knowledge to Siva.
audit_text_issue: 12 has one corrupt glyph in the praise.

note: Both hear the funeral drum over the corpse while kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still marries and seeks joy; 23 draws a different lesson, that one should share even a grain before the summons comes.
The Kural makes sharing one's food the chief of all duties; 23 arrives at the same act, sharing even a millet grain, through fear of death rather than compassion.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as a man's money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and in 33 the woman who melted him while wealth lasted beats him from the door when it ends.
audit_text_issue: 33 has a garbled word in the praise (மண்டுநநருர்).

note: Both turn desire away by showing the desired woman old. The Naladiyar gives one picture, the woman bent on her mother's staff; 34 takes each charm the songs praise, hair, eyes, breasts, and shows its ruin, then names a different remedy, service at the Lord's feet.
Both see the living body as a stinking corpse: the Naladiyar's cart torn by vultures once its axle breaks, and 30's body that already stinks, rots and rattles with worms and bones.
Both pray at the hour of death: 8 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's men strike, 28 that Death not call him while his body fails and his mother weeps, and that he reach the feet.

Both make evening the hour when love's sickness deepens; the Kural's woman says it bewilders the whole town, while in 24 a mother names the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird as what wears her daughter down.
Both bring a corpse into the courtesan's bed: in the Kural the man embracing her is embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 43 it is she who would embrace even a corpse for money.

Both list the body's insides, guts, blood, bone, sinews and skin, almost word for word (குடர், குருதி, என்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்). The Naladiyar turns the list on the desired woman; 48 turns it on the poet's own body, which he still fondles.

Both follow the drums of a funeral to the moment the body is left: the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead; 38 ends with the mourners leaving it on the road, and calls the whole scene mithya, a false life to escape.
Both ask Murugan to come on the peacock at the hour when Death's men arrive with the noose; 46 adds the kin following to the burning ground and asks above all to see his form.
The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, to be free of all other clinging; 54 asks, after confessing his infatuation, to attain clinging to Murugan (நின் பற்று அடைவேனோ).

Both name the Lord the eight-qualitied (எண்குணத்தான், எண்குணன்): the Kural makes the head that does not bow to his feet useless; in 52 the eight-qualitied Siva is himself the one who bows, worshipping Murugan.
audit_text_issue: 52 has unclear words in the first half (செஞ்செநீடும், அண்டுஞ்சகன்).

note: Both list the conventional comparisons for a woman's eyes, the carp, the lily, the spear. The Naladiyar names them as the talk of blind petty men to be ignored; 57 piles them up as the delusion that holds the poet, then asks to be freed of it.

The two songs are built alike: a confession that catalogues women's adornments, then a praise made of a chain of epithets ending -க்கார, each naming one role of Murugan. Read together they show the formula at work.
Tirumular warns against withering in praise of petty men for their wealth and bids one praise the Lord instead; 60 asks to give up praising impure men and to worship Murugan's feet.
Both quote the patron's flattery, the giver called a cloud and a lord of red or lotus hands. In 15 the poet confesses having begged so; in 55 he asks to keep such names for Murugan alone.

64 scorns poets who sing a girl's love-sickness, with Kama's arrows, the south wind and the crescent, without naming Thiruchendur; 24 uses the same devices, but for a girl in love with the lord of Senthil. The scorn falls on poems that leave out the shrine, not on the akam convention itself.
46 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's messengers drag the poet off; 63 asks further that he speak to Death and claim the man as his own devotee.

Both picture old age with speech failing, teeth gone and a staff in hand. The Naladiyar's old man still keeps his eyes on desire; in 68 the women laugh at him, and the poet turns the scene into a prayer for Murugan to come at the hour of death.
The Kural holds nothing more degrading to the tongue than asking; 69 confesses a tongue put to exactly that use, poems of praise carried from one patron's door to another.

Both list the poet's genres, கோவை, உலா, மடல் and the rest. In 69 they are tools for begging at patrons' doors; in 76 they are titles of honour and the source of the poet's pride, which he asks to have removed.
Both draw Death on his buffalo with noose and club and ask Murugan to come on the peacock at that hour; 75 grounds the claim in hereditary service, 8 in the confession that he has not served.
The Kural calls the embrace of deceiving women an அணங்கு, a possessing spirit; 73 gives the deceit a literal form, the love-pellets and the charm hidden in the betel.
audit_text_issue: 73's opening phrase is hard to divide.

note: The Kural puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; 88 joins two of the three in one figure, the courtesan who herself drinks palm toddy.
Both describe the yogi who binds the breath and tastes the nectar of bliss from the moon; Tirumular sets it against the liquor of fools, 94 against a life of delusion and the elements' illusions.
Both catalogue old age through the failing senses, cough and phlegm before death; 68 adds the mocking women and the family, 93 asks for more than rescue, the removal of Death's very principle.
Both confess wandering from door to door of worthless patrons with poems; 91 adds that Murugan himself is the true owner of the Tamil garlands the poet wasted.
76 asks to be rid of the poet's titles and honours as pride; 83 asks for the poet's title and fame, but only so that his service and song to Murugan may flourish.

Both put a woman's eye to a doubting question with Death among the answers. The Kural asks whether it is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three; 103 lengthens the list to poison, fish, Kama's arrow and Yama's messengers, and turns the doubt into the poet's own confusion before he asks for Murugan's feet.

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums while the kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still believes in household joy; 115 adds the mourners washing and letting go of the bond, and asks Murugan to come before that day.

Both say the paid embrace is false. The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in the dark; 111 shows it from inside, the price bargained, the tight embrace and the man melting like wax, and calls it a madness from which only release frees him.

The Naladiyar says those set on the right path will not embrace such women; 108 says their laughter makes even renouncers weaken. If 108's துறவினர் சோர is taken literally, it doubts the Naladiyar's confidence; it may be only the poet's hyperbole.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan: the moon that burns like the sun, Kama's arrows and the blaming women torment her, and the speaker asks him to come to her. 101 asks for his garland, 116 for his embrace on the peacock that is Om.

Both confess begging from patrons by praising them in Tamil. In 15 the plea is to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet; in 117 the begging is tied to desire for women and to the ruined body, and the fear is another birth.
Both identify Murugan with the Tamil saint who sent the Jains to the stakes at Madurai; 104 adds the cure of the king's fever, holy ash and Pugali, the details of Sambandar's story.
Both run a life in one breath from infancy to youth and desire for women. 9 begins in the womb and ends in disease; 110 stops at sixteen and names the omission, never praising the devotees' feet.

Both turn on a courtesan's vow never to part: the Naladiyar woman who promised to be like the gem on its thread turns like a ram's horn, and 121's women who swear union until death strip the man and go to meet the next. The Naladiyar asks the heart to leave; 121 asks Murugan to come.

The Kural cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe; 126 claims the eyes have beaten the deer into the forest and trampled Yama himself. The same comparisons, but the Kural's lover wonders and the poet of 126 fears to fall.
audit_text_issue: Several lines of 126's first half are compressed and hard to split; the marker flags uncertainty.

note: Both set Murugan against Death's buffalo and noose at the hour of death; 8 asks him to come on the peacock, 129 asks that Death not come near at all and adds the jackals and fire that claim the corpse.
Both are confessions of worship never done, built as a list of negatives (தொழுதிலன், சேவித்தறியேனே); 8 ends at the hour of death, 123 at the wish to end birth.
Both give Murugan the impaling of the Jains, the Madurai story told of Sambandar: 17 names the Tamil mouth that set them on stakes, 132 has him settle at Palani after seeing them there.
12 praises Murugan for giving the knowledge to Siva; 133 asks whether the poet, as a servant, will receive the same teaching of the Veda's meaning.
audit_text_issue: 12 has a corrupt glyph in கி஡ணவ (likely கிரீவ).

note: Both confess begging from patrons: 15 praises them in Tamil with a wounded heart, 134 stands without shame at the gates of those who give food. 134 sets the begging at the end of a life that runs from the womb through women.

Both reject the poets' comparisons for a woman's eyes as carp, spear and the like: the Naladiyar ascetic answers them with the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit, 135 asks not to drown in their maya and turns to studying Murugan's poems.
audit_text_issue: 135 line 4 has corrupt characters (பா஡ண, இ஧ல்முழ்).

note: Tirumular says that if one knows how to reach the inner light there is no quarrel at all; 138 lists the clamouring schools and asks for the teaching and vision of knowledge that would end the dispute for him.
Both open with the sects that cannot agree and ask Murugan for knowledge and his feet instead; 124 adds the ash, 138 names the schools one by one.

The Kural's பொதுநலத்தார், women whose favours are common to all, are 141's women who set a price so that all may take their pleasure; the Kural says the wise will not touch them, 141 confesses that he did.
The Kural calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire in which base men sink; 144 confesses to desiring those golden shoulders and sinking low (தாழ்வடைந்து).

Both list the body's contents, guts, fat, blood, bone and flesh. The Naladiyar asks where among them the garlanded woman is; 145 applies the list to the body the poet himself lives in, and answers with the Lord's grace.
Both give Murugan a deed of Sambandar: 132 the impaling of the Jains, 137 the milk of Parvati given to the child who then sang Tamil.

Both name Seypathi (Vayalur) as the place where Murugan acted on the poet: in 149 he stopped him and made him his servant, in 152 he gave him the love of singing Thiruppugazh daily. Read together they are the book's account of its own beginning.

Both hear the funeral drums and see the body covered and the fire taken up. The Naladiyar ends in irony, the dying carrying the dead; 157 asks for release before that hour comes, while the hut of the body still stands.

Both take the body apart into blood, bone, nerves, skin and flesh. The Naladiyar asks which part is the woman one desires; 158 turns the list on the poet's own body and confesses that, knowing this, he still desires women.

Both place the soul's bondage at conception: Tirumular has maya join the soul in the womb, turiya broken and karma take hold; 160 has the form grow in the womb from seed and breath, divided by the three gunas and covered in deceit, and contrasts it with the turiya state of the liberated.

The Kural's first line makes A the first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 163 borrows the words (அகர முதல்) and asks for the meaning that is first in that way, the secret that 173 says Murugan told Siva.

Both are love-laments in the same short metre over a lovesick girl, worn down by Kama's arrows, the sea or south wind, and evening; both name Murugan as the one who spoke a word to Siva. 24 is plainly the mother's voice; 164 asks Murugan for his garland for the girl.

Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons for gifts. 15 regrets it with a wounded heart and asks for service instead; 175 adds the patrons' contempt and asks whether men who do not think of Murugan deserve to be sung at all.
Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains, who are impaled, and with the holy ash: in 149 the ash is spread through the town, in 171 a pinch of it cures the Pandya king.
audit_text_issue: 171's confession lines are partly unclear.

note: 153 alludes to the race round the world in one line; 176 tells the whole story, including Murugan's anger at losing the fruit, and makes it the reason he dwells at Palani.
audit_text_issue: 176 line 2 has corrupt characters (தன஧முவ).

note: The Kural warns of women who weigh the profit and then speak of their goodness; 172 describes the same pretence from inside, women who take every possession 'with great friendship'.
Both make a man's welcome depend on what he brings: the Naladiyar's courtesans find a moneyed oil-presser sugar, and 178's women question at the door those who come with property and carry it off.

Both say the courtesan's sweet talk serves her wish for wealth, not love. The Kural states it as a warning; 180 shows the sequence, talk, trust, then the wealth snatched, and asks for the Lord's love in its place.

Both raise the breath from the root through the channel between ida and pingala to the head and arrive at the Lord's feet. Tirumular states the method; 188 asks for it as a gift, and hears the goal as the anklet sound of the dancing foot.
audit_text_issue: 188's நாலங்குலம் and சிகாரம் lines are obscure.

note: 27 asks to see how to leave the embrace and gain the feet; 190 describes the same embrace and vows not to forget the feet even there. Read as a vow, 190 allows a remembrance inside desire that 27 seeks by leaving it.

Both set the Lord above the alchemist's work. Tirumular makes the five-letter mantra the alchemist's pill that turns the body to gold; 194 says mercury and the nine metals end as charcoal, while knowing Murugan as the gem brings everything.
Both tell the poet's life as one arc from the womb and the breast to the houses of women. 181 adds Brahma sending the soul out to eat its deeds; 195 adds the age of sixteen and the wealth lost.
Both make weeping the sign of devotion: Tirumular melts in love and cries day and night, and 199 asks to wear the feet on his head and weep and weep for grace.
Both songs of Avinankudi call Murugan the giver of போதகம், the teaching: 179 opens by hailing him as such, and 200 ends with Siva bowing to receive it.

Tirumular teaches breath held on the left so that the body does not decay; 211 asks to be rid of the anxious yoga that turns back the breath because it will not accept that the body must go, and seeks silence instead. The conflict holds if 211's participles describe the yoga it rejects, which is the likelier reading.
audit_text_issue: Two corrupt glyphs in 211 (அனலு஡தி, புண்ட஡ணகம்)

note: Both use the string-puppet for a life with no inner agency: in the Kural the man without shame only seems alive, in 207 the poet dances on the strings of his two deeds.
Tirumular says the knowers perceive Siva within the soul 'like a painting'; 212's obscure plea for the end 'in the painting' may ask for the same still perception.
audit_text_issue: 212's ஓவியத்தில் அந்தம் and தூமமேய்க் கணிந்த are obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: Both complain of the poet's life at patrons' gates: 210 of the men who slip away once praised in song, 220 of genres wasted on fools who toss a coin; both turn to the Lord's feet instead.

The Naladiyar gives one picture, a pot of filth leaking from nine openings under a dark skin; 217 takes the body apart organ by organ and disease by disease, and adds the hut of five elements taken up birth after birth.
audit_text_issue: 217 has garbled words (சங்முளை, வங்க்முடே).

note: The Kural finds the body's joy in touching one's children; 218 asks for that very joy with the Lord as the child on the lap, and puns the child's kiss (முத்தி) into release.
Both are songs of a girl lovesick for Murugan, voiced by someone near her, with the evening moon and Kama's arrows; 221 adds the street's gossip.
Tirumular counts the Agamas twenty-eight, heard from Siva; 223 asks for the release that runs through the same twenty-eight, so the plea rests on the Siddhanta canon.
Both call the courtesan's embrace false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், பொய்க்கலவி) because it is for wealth; the Kural likens it to a corpse in a dark room, 227 adds poison and wealth snatched.

The Kural says one who neither gives nor enjoys has nothing however rich; 239 is the confession of such a man, who kept his wealth for his hands and youth and shared nothing with the hungry, and finds it at the funeral.
Both set sharing food against the funeral drum and the wailing kin: 23 resolves to share even a grain before the summons, 239 confesses that he never did.

Both put the courtesan's embrace for money in a dark room (இருட்டறை). The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse; 252 keeps the room and the seized wealth but not the corpse, and confesses the pull instead of warning.

Both take the body apart into bone, blood, fat and entrails to break desire. The Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman; 248 turns the inventory on the poet's own body, a house he still longs to carry.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons in Tamil for gifts; 245 adds the rebuff, 'come tomorrow' and the turned face, and asks, like 15, for the feet instead.
Both are catalogues of diseases set as the plea; 232 ties them to sin and women, while 243 asks to be spared them in every birth.
audit_text_issue: 232 has a corrupt word in line 12 (வெற஧முடி).

note: Both name the Thiruppugazh within itself as a means of grace: 242 says reading it cuts affliction, 249 asks to live among those who sing it.

Tirumular says the eaters of flesh are seized by Yama's messengers and thrown into hell; 247 counts the daily eating of killed flesh among the bonds and asks for release from them, without the threat.
audit_text_issue: 247 has garbled readings (த்ததகுரு, encoding glitch in கொலு஡னை).

note: Both say the six sects lead back to birth: in Tirumular they perish where they stand, not knowing the way to leave the earth, and in 257 the sectarians who install many gods wander only to enter the womb again.
audit_text_issue: TM 1535 'முண்ணின் றழியு' looks corrupt (perhaps உண்ணின்று).

note: Both call the body a pot to turn the mind from women. The Naladiyar's pot is the woman's body seeping filth; 258 turns the image on the poet's own body, a false pot of flesh, skin and semen, and asks not just to leave desire but to have that birth cut off.

Both make the town's gossip feed love's sickness: the Kural's woman calls it the manure of her disease, and in 262 the women's talk is one of the torments, with cuckoo, moon and sea, that waste the girl's arm.
Both laments end by asking Murugan to give the wasting girl his garland; 265 calls it a garland of compassion, so the love token becomes grace.
The same formula of the courtesan's love that lasts as long as the money: in 33 the man is beaten from the door when it ends, in 266 he is left groaning there.
audit_text_issue: 266: ஡ணங்கிசை corrupt; 33: மண்டுநநருர் garbled.

note: Both identify Murugan with Sambandar defeating the Jains: 261 tells the cure of the Pandyan and the crushing of the Jains, 263 the impaling.
audit_text_issue: 261: கடலு஡டே has corrupt glyph.

note: The Kural makes the Lord's feet the way across the great sea of births; 284 makes them a raft (புணை) and adds two more seas to cross, desire for women and the arts of learning.
Both say learning without knowledge of the Lord leaves one a fool; 279 confesses it in the first person, having read Vedas and Puranas and mocked the silent knowers as dumb.
Both measure the Lord by breadth and length and find no measure: Tirumular asks who knows them, and 279 names the reality whose breadth and length cannot be told, which the poet's learning scorned.
Both take the body apart as a false pot, a bellows and a home of diseases, and both ask not for health but for the end of the birth that brings such a body.
Both make the Thiruppugazh itself what saves: 269 gives it the power to end birth, and 277 asks that devotees live speaking it without forgetting.

Both are laments for a girl in love with Murugan, with the moon, the south wind and Kama's arrows as what wears her down; 24 is a mother's grief, 286 adds the town's women quarrelling in the street and asks for the god's garland.
Both confess begging praise of patrons in the language of gods and clouds; 292 goes further, quoting the poet comparing a poor patron to the six-faced Murugan himself, the god he should have praised.

Tirumular says the women and children who ate from the house do not follow the dead; 298 asks for that knowledge in advance, that wife, children, mother and goods become alien to the mind before the buffalo comes.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood, knowing grey hair will come; 296 is the prayer of one who did not, asking even when his hair is grey and his body ripens and falls to be taken into the supreme light.
The Kural makes women of divided heart the company of those whom Fortune has left; 299 lives the sequence, infatuation, all money given away, then hunger burning in the belly.
Both close by naming the poet's own work at Thanigai: 299 has Murugan delight in the Tamil garland of Arunagirinathan, and 301 has Thanigai as the place where those who chant Thiruppugazh gather.
audit_text_issue: 301's battle line has a garble (புநக்முள).

note: Both renounce the poet's trade of praising patrons; 292 quotes the comparisons he made, and 306 names the misers and the bards' claim that they are Pari and Kari, and asks instead for one word from Murugan.

The Kural begs those who beg not to beg of those who hide what they have; 306 confesses doing exactly that, praising misers as generous, and its answer is not to choose better patrons but to give patrons up for Murugan.
Both make Murugan the Tamil poet who sent the Jains to the stake, i.e. Sambandar; 299 adds the woman's husband brought back, 306 the Pandya's hunch and fever cured by the holy ash.
audit_text_issue: 299 has மிக்முள, probably மிக்குள.

note: Tirumular teaches that bindu and nada, raised in the body, join in samadhi; 305 uses the same terms but says the state cannot be reached even by jnanis and silent sages, and asks Murugan to come and give it.
Both confess the poet's begging trade, praising patrons as wishing trees and clouds; 310 adds the name of the Sangam giver Kumanan and calls the flattery a blind theft of the words owed to the Lord.
Tirumular says the Lord is not the thing the six sects hold; 314 makes him the truth hard for the six sects who quarrel daily, and yet the common ground (பொது) that holds all.

Both set the Lord who is one with everything yet apart against the confusion of the six sects; 257 mocks their images and wealth, 314 their angry argument, and asks to teach the truth in every direction.
Both see through the bubble: the Naladiyar's body is a bubble in the rain that forms and bursts, while 316 sees the whole world (ப்ரபஞ்சம்) as a bubble, and asks for the ripeness to reach the Lord.

Both picture the old man with failing speech or senses, leaning on a stick, staggering, teeth gone; the Naladiyar's still has eyes for desire, while 319 adds the disgust of his kin and wife and asks for the feet before that day.
Both picture the poet's old age with stick, white hair and loose teeth while others mock; 68 asks Murugan to come at the hour of death, 319 to reach the feet before that despised birth.
Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, wounded by Kama's flower arrows and a burning moon, and ask him to come with his garland; 337 adds that the moon rose with the poison of the sea.

Both are laments for a lovesick girl in another's voice, with the classical torments of the evening world: 24 the anril bird, south wind and crescent, 334 the roaring sea and the crescent seized by the serpent.

The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; 329 asks for the clinging that does not suffer, set against the clinging to food and wealth, if its line is divided so.
Both have the heirs at the deathbed thinking of property: in 68 the young sons ask about debts and goods, in 324 the kin cry 'a little for me, a little for you' over the wealth and gold plate.
Both confess worshipping patrons for gold; 310 tells the flattery at length, 331 sets the patrons' feet (தருவோர் தாள்) against the Lord's in a few beats.
audit_text_issue: 331's doubled syllables make the first lines' division uncertain.

note: Both picture old age by teeth lost and a body bent on a stick. The Naladiyar uses it against the old man who still desires; 341 carries the picture on to the corpse burned and the kin going home.

Both are laments in another voice for a girl lovesick for Murugan, worn down by the night's sights and sounds: in 24 the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird, in 344 the stained moon and the roaring sea.
The Kural warns that women who desire a man for his wealth bring him harm; 345 tells the harm from inside, the wealth given away and a poverty that burns like the undersea fire.

Tirumular, by Nandi's command, promises that breath tied fast keeps the body for thousands of years; 355 calls the yogi who holds the breath to make the impermanent flesh last a fool. The conflict holds if 722 is read as bodily longevity sought for its own sake and 355 as rejecting that practice, not only its misuse.
Both say the courtesan desires the wealth and not the man; 357 sharpens it into a measure, the desire acted exactly as far as the gold goes.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising unworthy patrons for gold: 352 tells it in summary, 358 quotes the begging speech itself, the boast of prosody and the call for jewels.
Both take the body apart into entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin. The Naladiyar asks which part is the desired woman; 362 makes the inventory the hut in which the poet's own senses run wild.
Both speak of the Absolute by what cannot reach it: 347 by learning, the mind, the tattvas and the Vedas, 359 by chariyai, kiriyai and the turiya state.

Both see the sects as people wandering off, each crying its own 'this is supreme'. Tirumular's remedy is to go the ordained way and seek the King; 369's is to melt in devotion and drop 'mine', when the reality the Vedas proclaim is easily gained.

Both use the Kural's word for courtesans (வரைவிலா, வரைவில்) and picture their pleasure as something a man sinks into: the Kural's mire (அளறு), 370's sea of pleasure, which 370 sets against a second sea, the bliss of Siva.
Both make the courtesan a woman who weighs: in the Kural she weighs the profit and speaks of her virtue to match, in 373 she measures her heart to the money (திரவியம் அளவளவு அளவியர்).

Both end the plea with the same vow, not to forget the word and the two feet given at Arunai; 371 confesses every pleasure first, 373 every deceit of the women, and both keep the vow inside the confession.

The Kural's lover discovers that Death has a woman's eyes, half in wonder; 374 extends the discovery to every charm, breasts as Yama and the pearls on them as Yama's rope, and turns it into a reason to turn away.
Both open the hour of death with the same formula, Yama casting his thick-handed noose (பரியகைப் பாசம் விட்டு எறியும்); 376 asks for the life to be saved, 378 for the fault to be forgiven.
Both count the flute among the torments of the lovesick woman: the Kural's herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills, and 380's sweet lone flute is one of four things she asks to survive.
Both quote the courtesan's invitation, 'come to my house' (21's இங்கு நின்றது என் வீடே, 384's அருகு வீடு இதுதான் அதில் வாரும்); 384 adds that it is spoken to men of wealth and sworn on oaths.
audit_text_issue: 21 has garbled words (வா஡ண, நநடுர் கேர்டுர்).

note: Both give a woman's eyes the power to eat the life of those who look: the Kural's lover says it of one girl with wonder, 386 of women's eyes in general, likened to Siva's throat-poison and Murugan's vel.
Both liken women's eyes to poison and end with Murugan hiding his own form to follow the hunter girl; 387 takes the simile further, to the poison of the churned sea that cracked the cosmic egg.
Both stage the death-bed with wife and sons weeping before Yama comes; 376 asks for the life to be saved, 388 for knowledge to clear his troubles so that he can think of the feet.
audit_text_issue: 388's opening (இரவியு மதியுந் தெரிவுற எழுமம் புவி) is of uncertain sense.

note: Both set the uproar of the sects (கோலாகலச் சமயம், கலக விபரித பர சமயிகள்) against a knowledge they cannot reach: 369's reality without birth or death, 394's seal of silence.
audit_text_issue: 394 line 1 garbled (தொழுத்மு டூடு, கடலு஡டுற்).

note: Both make the town's talk feed the girl's love-sickness: in the Kural gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water, in 397 the town reproaches her alongside the north wind.

Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as the money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and 398's women of magic arts cling only as far as the wealth goes (பொருளது அளவும் மருவுறு).

Both call the body a pot (கும்பம்) of filth: the Naladiyar's pot seeps through nine openings under its dark skin, 402's is a pot where stench and liquor pool. The Naladiyar turns the image on the desired woman; 402 turns it on the poet's own body.

Both describe the embrace in full and then refuse to forget the feet within it: 403 says 'even then I will never forget', 420 asks 'even in union, will I forget your golden feet?'. Unlike most of the book, they ask for remembrance, not escape.
Both use the evening torments of love, the moon and Kama's arrows, for a girl in love with Murugan. In 24 her mother speaks; in 404 the girl herself asks him to come before she dies.

Both describe the same yoga: kindling the fire and raising it until the nectar of the moon is drunk. Tirumular calls those who do it Siva-yogis; 405 confesses that the poet has not done it and wanders after women instead.
Both list the foods Ganapati takes, gram or dal, sesame, plantains and other fruits; in 2 they lead into the poet's call to sing, in 409 into pure praise.
audit_text_issue: 2 has a corrupt word in the offering list (தன஧முலம்).

note: Both show the old man with failing speech and a staff. The Naladiyar's still keeps his eyes on desire; 412 follows the man spent on courtesans to the end, deaf and on a mat, while his own wife, children and kin call him a curse.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, tormented by Kama's five flower arrows, and ask him to come with his garland; 101 is spoken for her, 413 by her, and adds that one night feels like an age.
Both run a life from the embryo in the womb through birth, nursing and crawling to desire for women. 9 ends in disease; 423 counts learning among the stages, calling it empty knowledge.
audit_text_issue: 423's praise has a garbled name (likely Vibhishana)

note: Tirumular lists the rotations of the five-letter mantra in order from SI: சிவயநம, மசிவயந, நமசிவய, யநமசிவ, வயநமசி. 425 chants the same rotations in the same order, each joined to the name of Arunachala, making a teaching of the mantra into a hymn to the hill.

Both make Murugan the Tamil saint who sent the Jains of Madurai to the stakes. 104 adds Pugali and the cure of the king's fever; 426 adds the milk the mountain's daughter gave, the other mark of Sambandar's story.

Both show vultures tearing at the body. The Naladiyar's stinking cart is shown to men who praise sandal and garlands; 422 sees the poet's own body as the feast of dogs, jackals, vultures and worms, and turns from it to the company of devotees.

The Kural says neither the shaved head nor long matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 428 confesses to both marks, the shaved head and the grown locks, with the condemned conduct, the hunt for gold, kept underneath.
Tirumular says the false garb is worn for the sake of eating; in 428 the poet confesses to wearing it to make gold, and asks for pity rather than claiming the garb.

Both list the same diseases (scrofula, the great belly, phlegm, colic, urinary flux). 243 asks that they not afflict him through his births; 441 gives up on the body and asks instead for Siva-knowledge and the power to sing the Thiruppugazh.

Tirumular says the form grows ten months, comes into the world in its season and grows mingled with maya, and asks who knows how. 444 follows that same growth month by month to birth in the tenth, and then on past it to the pyre.
audit_text_issue: 444's embryo passage is hard to divide.

note: Both hear the funeral drum while kin wail over the corpse; the Naladiyar's drum mocks the living, while 444 notes that the kin weep each for their own share.
audit_text_issue: 444's embryo and battle passages are hard to divide.

note: Both end the cherished body as carrion: the Naladiyar's vultures tear the stinking cart once its axle breaks, and 446 lays the householder in a pit for vultures and dogs. The Naladiyar's target is the praise of perfumes and garlands; 446's is family life.
audit_text_issue: 446's opening (சரக்கேறித் தப்பதி, பரிக்காயம், குரக்கோணம்) is obscure.

note: Both give the courtesan's course in one sequence: the Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from a man's hands and then balks like an ox; 458's coaxes, takes gold until the wealth is gone, then drives him off with deceitful words.
Both carry the courtesan song past the bed to the diseases it leaves, sores with pus and festering; 456 follows them into Death's city, 461 to the onlookers who cover their eyes.

Both see the body as a bubble that forms and bursts; the Naladiyar praises the firm who resolve from this to end their wandering, and 469 asks from it for the one release complete in wisdom, silence and bliss.
The Kural makes the letter A first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 467 takes the letter itself as a name of the Goddess, calling Sivakami the அகரம் and the life of all.

Both ask not to leave the bed but to hold the Lord there: 468 vows to keep the twelve eyes and twelve arms even while sporting with women, and 467 asks for the moon faces and feet in the same embrace.
Both make poverty the end of the courtesan's love: the Naladiyar's flood ends when the income ends, and 477's women first show delusion and then show poverty.

Both join the catalogue of the body's diseases to the ninety-six tattvas living off the body; 487 adds the house-building and desire for wealth that keep the poet from the space where the peacock dances.
Tirumular counts the ninety-six as tenants of a walled temple who run off when it falls; 487 makes the same ninety-six the eaters of the body, a picture of consumption rather than desertion.
audit_text_issue: 487 has the corrupt glyph ஡ in லு஡சல்.

note: Both turn the body into a dwelling whose real occupants are diseases, listed at length; 485 names the fault as taking that dwelling for permanent.

Tirumular's Siva-jnanis go about as dead while their senses and body remain; 490 asks for exactly this, the goal won by dying in the mind before the body is carried to the burning ground, but offers the Lord the alternative of living on in understanding.

The Naladiyar says it matters nothing whether the body is dragged, buried or thrown away once its dweller has left; 493 lists the same receivers of the corpse, vultures, jackals, fire and earth, but as weary claimants, so that the repetition across countless births is itself the burden.

Both are laments for a girl sick with love for Murugan, told by another voice, with the wind, the birds and the signs of evening wearing her down; 24 is the mother's, and 488 asks Murugan for his garland.
audit_text_issue: 488's வருகொவே looks corrupt (வருகோவே).

note: Both make the courtesan's only question whose money there is: the Naladiyar's women find even an oil-presser sweet if he has wealth, and 481's women, with hearts dry as cane waste, think only whose wealth it will be.

The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 497 asks to be spared ochre, matted hair, forest wandering and fasting and to be given instead the inner knowledge in which the self subsides. Both set the ascetic's outward marks aside, the Kural for conduct, 497 for grace and knowledge.
Both run a life from the womb through infancy and youth to women and then decline without pause; 9 ends in disease, 508 in Death's arrival, and both ask for release from the cycle.

Both picture the body as food for scavengers: Naladiyar 48 has vultures tearing the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 510 the ghoul, the dog and the fly. The Naladiyar uses it to shame those who praise the body; 510 asks to be taken out of it into release.

Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums (பறை), and both make the funeral a lesson: Naladiyar 24 notes that the dying carry the dead; 512 sets the funeral at the end of a life spent on courtesans.

Both speakers address their own mind (நெஞ்சே, மனமே) and urge it to set out with them on the good path. Naladiyar 55 gives the reason as youth wasted and old age coming; 513 gives only the Lord, who cuts the root of impurity.

Both begin the life with a drop like dew (பனிபோல், பனியின் விந்துளி) and follow it head down out of the womb to the crawling child; 508 goes on to women and Death, 520 to past deeds and a ruined mind.

Both look ahead to grey hair and the staff and draw the lesson that one should act before they come: the Naladiyar praises those who renounced in childhood, 524 asks to serve the Lord's servants before the body ripens.
The two songs end with the same two lines, Murugan dwelling on the Venkatam hill and giving his devotees whatever they ask when they ask it; a formula of this shrine.

Both see the body as a bag full of holes (Naladiyar தொளைபலவாய், 534 தொள்ளைப் புலாற்பை). The Naladiyar tells the lover to look at the desired body as a bag turned inside out; 534 turns the image on the poet's own body and asks to be rid of it.
Both take the poet's body apart as a list of containers, pot, bellows and bag in 280, a dozen kinds of bag in 534, and both ask for the end of that body rather than its health.
audit_text_issue: 534's bag-words (ஞெள்ளற்பை, துராற்பை) and praise are obscure.

note: Both songs call the body கள்வைத்த தோற்பை, a skin bag holding toddy, a formula the poet reuses. In 534 it is one of a dozen bags; 536 sets it against the formless form seen by the inner eye.
audit_text_issue: 536 has மொழிக்தரு, probably corrupt.

note: Both set the sect-disputers' learning aside: 124 opens with sectarians who cannot see one another's truth, 535 asks not to be tossed in the wrangling of the six sects' logicians. 535's reading rests on one clear line in a dense song.
audit_text_issue: 535 is dense rhythmic text whose word division is largely conjectural.

note: Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, tormented by the moon and the breeze, and ask him for his garland as the cure; 537 adds a plea that he not blame her old karma.

Both picture a man who clings to house and desire into a failing old age. The Naladiyar's old man, toothless on his staff, still has his eyes on desire and so has no path to safety; 541's clings to children and gold until he is grey and breathless, and asks for grace before Yama's rope catches him.

Both open with a riddle of what a woman's eye is, a string of 'or's of weapons, poison and fish. In 103 Yama's messengers are one of the answers; 546 keeps them out of the list and sets them, with club and noose, at the end of the plea.

Both make the courtesan's welcome depend on the gift in hand. The Naladiyar's women would send away even Vishnu with folded hands if he brought nothing; 550's will not speak to a man on the day he brings no gold.

Both picture the courtesan's double dealing as a body turned to more than one man at once: the Naladiyar's eel shows its head to the snake and its tail to the fish; 553 gives the eyes to one man, the breasts to another, the hands to a third.
audit_text_issue: 553 has a corrupt glyph in வயலு஡ரா.

note: Both show Yama's servants binding the soul with ropes and driving it into fire. Tirumular gives the punishment to those who urged killing; 558 names no sin, and lists the tortures at length only to ask Murugan to end them.
audit_text_issue: 558 has the corrupt glyph ஡ in அனலு஡டே.

note: Both describe the Lord as beyond speech and conduct: Tirumular's great one is beyond speech, word and feeling (பேசா உரையுணர்வற்ற); 561's Reality cannot be read, worshipped or spoken (வாய்விட்டுப் பேசொணாதது).
audit_text_issue: 561 reads போசொணாதது for பேசொணாதது, and வயலு஡ரத்தில் has a corrupt glyph.

note: Both measure women's charms by their effect on ascetics: in 108 their laughter makes renouncers weaken (துறவினர் சோர), in 563 their breasts make the ascetics of the great principle faint (தத்துவத்துத் தவர் சோர), the same verb.

Both list the tortures Yama's messengers inflict, binding, dragging, burning. 558 lists them without a reason; 564 gives them one, an account of the poet's deeds opened and totalled, with the torture matched to the sum.
audit_text_issue: 558 has corrupt glyph in அனலு஡டே; 564's opening splits are uncertain.

note: Both call the courtesan's body a mire (அளறு) into which men sink; the Kural's word also means hell, and 574 asks to be taken by the Lord so as not to sink there.
audit_text_issue: Last two lines of 574's praise nearly repeat each other (வழியருளின் பேறு காட்டி)

note: Both counter desire by naming the body's openings and their seepage: the Naladiyar's pot oozing filth from nine holes, 574's rotting, cloth-stopped hole. The Naladiyar calls the lover a fool; 574 asks for rescue.
audit_text_issue: 574's text has obscure lines (இறைவைகொளுங் கூவல், சீலை தீற்று) and the last two praise lines nearly repeat each other.

note: Both make the woman's eye Death: the Kural's lover cannot tell if her look is Death, an eye or a doe, while 578 calls the eye-corners Yama's messengers in a confession it was saved from.

Both say rites and recitation do not yield the truth: Tirumular's men perform many rites and recite hymns yet wither without understanding; 573 doubts that japa, fire-offerings and Agamic learning passed down by gurus can be a refuge without Siva's own gift.

Both define Sivayoga. Tirumular makes it knowing the conscient and non-conscient and becoming one's own light; 575 makes it seeing every element, scripture, letter and god abide as one form, and adds that the malas must go first.

27 asks to see clearly how to leave the embrace and reach the feet; 582 vows to remember the feet even asleep on the breasts after union, so devotion is placed inside desire rather than after it, if the vow is not read as hyperbole.

Both confess the court poet's begging: 579 praised the man who never gives as Kubera, 589 sang correct Tamil verse to iron-hearted men who show no pity. Both make this, not only desire, a reason he did not seek the Lord.

The Kural says nothing degrades the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; 589 shows that degradation in the poet himself, trembling and cringing as he sings for gifts, and asks whether such a tongue can gain love for the Lord.
Both thank Murugan for the grace of being told to sing the Thiruppugazh (செப்பென); 2 lists what the song must hold, and 602 already hears it recited by devotees in all four directions.

The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; 603 confesses exactly that folly, living as if a bubble-like life with wife, sons and house would stand for a crore of aeons.
Both see life as a bubble (புற்புதம்). The Naladiyar praises those who see it so and resolve to end their wandering; 603 confesses that he knows the image and still lives as if it lasted.
8 asks Murugan to come on the peacock when Death's men strike and end his fear; 605 turns the same hour into a battle the servant wins with Murugan's grace, and asks him to come and watch.
The Kural names double-hearted women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom fortune has left; 609 opens its list with gamblers and money-loving women side by side and adds disease.

15 confesses that the poet himself begged from patrons, praising them as clouds in giving; 613 looks at the same trade from outside, at poets who praise men as the cloud-dark Vishnu and steal verses, and disowns their way.
Both give the courtesan's vow of oneness and show it false: the Naladiyar's woman swore never to part, like gem and thread, and turned away; 626's women swear 'you are me and I am you' without shame.
8 asks Murugan to come when Death's servants strike; 625 shows those same servants trembling at his vel, so the fear of the plea is answered in the praise.

Both are love-sickness told with the moon, Kama's arrows and the cuckoo; 14 names the speaker as a deceiver longing for women, while 628 leaves its speaker unnamed and ends on Valli at Murugan's chest.
Both picture the poet laughed at by his own: in 610 wife, town and kin mock him, in 631 mother, kin and clan laugh as disease wastes his body; both answer by asking to be drawn to the Lord.
Both describe women who take the wealth from a man's hand once he is caught; the Naladiyar adds that he is laughed at, 633 that his very strength of mind is destroyed.
Both confess the humiliation of pleading before patrons; 15 tells the flattery, 632 says he can no longer bear to plead his poverty to base and cruel men after women took his wealth.
The Kural says only those who join the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; 634 asks in the same image whether he will swim the long wave of birth and reach the pure feet.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, wounded by Kama's flowers and burned by the moon, and plead with him for her: 337 asks for his garland, 645 that he come and give her life, adding the tears she weeps as pearls through the night.

The Kural's woman hears the cowherd's flute as the herald of a burning evening and a weapon that kills; in 647 the cowherds' bamboo flute is one of the evening torments, with the sea and the moon, of a girl sick for Murugan.
Both place sayujya past the ordinary states of consciousness: Tirumular calls it reaching the state beyond waking and becoming Siva; 643 sets it above turiya and beyond every path and sect.
audit_text_issue: 643 has a garble, சுகசெர்ருபத்தை for சுகசொரூபத்தை.

note: Both trace the embryo growing through the sizes of a seed, palm fruit and coconut and slipping head down into the world, a formula the book repeats; 520 goes on to virtue forgotten and a stinking body, 652 to the women who ruin the grown child.
Both make the ten months in the womb the start of bondage: Tirumular's form grows mingled with maya, and 652's child, grown by the way of deeds, ends among women.

Both define the giver by his shame at the word 'none': the Kural's man of good family does not utter the misery of 'I have nothing' and gives without refusing, and 662 names those ashamed to say 'there is none', who do not refuse from what they have, using the same word for misery (எவ்வம்).
The Kural calls the palmyra horse the only defence of those who suffer in love; 664 has Murugan himself, infatuated in Valli's field, mount it, the god taking the lover's last resort.
audit_text_issue: Several phrases of 664 (வாராய்பதி காதங் காதரை ஒன்முரும்) are obscure or corrupt.

note: Both take the body apart into its stuff, skin, flesh, blood and bone: the Naladiyar to ask which part is the desired woman, 665 to show the hut the life lives in before it asks for the strength to praise.

Both make the courtesan's welcome depend on the gift: the Naladiyar's women send away even Mal if his hand is empty, and 666's women show delight to the man who gives much and drive off one who does not.
audit_text_issue: 666 has two corrupt glyphs (ஊறல்கள், வேலூர்).

note: 653 gives Sambandar's defeat of the Jains as one epithet of Murugan; 666 tells the whole Madurai episode, the ash on the king, the hump straightened, the leaf against the current, as Murugan's deed.

Both make a single handful of food for the hungry the measure of dharma; 671 confesses the poet did not give even that one handful (ஒருபிடி) while he spent himself on courtesans, where Tirumular sets it as what anyone can do.

Both confess the poet's trade of singing to patrons who do not deserve it; 358 quotes the begging speech, 677 asks only whether he must go on giving endless songs to sinners blind to the Lord's protection.

Both set vultures on the body to answer its admirers: the Naladiyar shows them tearing at the stinking cart once its axle breaks, 679 calls the living body the hut they will feed on and makes it the reason to stop carrying it from town to town.
Both warn that the courtesan's sweet words serve her wish for wealth; 683 shows the words in action, the talk of old intimacy leading to the house where the wealth is plundered.

Both are akam songs in another voice built from the classical torments of the lovesick girl, the moon and Kama's arrows; 24 is the mother's lament for her daughter, 693 is the girl's own plea that the god come to her bed.

Both set marriage and the household inside the march to the burning ground: the Naladiyar mocks the man who sees the corpse carried yet marries and thinks there is joy here, and 700 lists embracing women and bearing the household's burden between crawling and burning.
Both tell the courtesan's cycle to its end, the man welcomed while his wealth lasts and then beaten and driven out; 702 adds the bargaining at the start and the new man taken up afterwards.
audit_text_issue: 33's praise has the garbled word மண்டுநநருர்.

note: Twin songs in one metre: both walk a life from the womb through childhood, women and the hunt for wealth, and both end in the same plea for love that reaches the feet before one falls into hell. 704 dwells longer on infancy (the birth rite, crawling), 703 on youth and roaming.
audit_text_issue: 703 line 4 is garbled (பாழவெளநேரகெய் தாம).

note: Both condemn the man who begrudges another's giving: the Kural says his kin will be left without food or clothing, and 707 puts him among those who fall into Yama's pit.
The Kural says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; 707 lists those who forget the good done them among the brutes who fall into Yama's pit, giving that 'no escape' a place.

Both make the stilled and turned breath the end of dying: Tirumular says that when breath stays with the mind there is no birth or death, and 709 asks that, with the breath turned into the skull and samadhi gained, the endless dying cease.

Both make the Lord's feet the way across the sea of births: the Kural says only those who join his feet swim it, and 718 calls the twin lotus feet a raft (புணை) to be grasped instead of the leaking body.
audit_text_issue: 718: உதிதாம்பரத்தை line obscure.

note: Both see the courtesan's sweetness as aimed at a man's money: the Kural warns that such women's sweet words bring harm, and 723 shows the flattery on the bed with the hand already reaching for the purse.

Both use the courtesan's being common to all as the charge: the Kural's women 'whose goodness belongs to everyone' (பொதுநலத்தார்) and 730's பொதுவிகள். The Kural says the wise don't plunge in; 730 is the confession of one who did.
The Kural's women weigh the profit and then speak of virtue; 731's women have minds set on the coin and lying speech. Both make the calculation the mark of the courtesan.

Tirumular says that for those who hold Nandi in love there is no caste; 731 asks that the lowness of being sunk in caste and clan end when he reaches the feet. Both place caste among what falls away at release.

Both make silence the door of release: Tirumular says release comes to those to whom silence has come and all speech ends, and 734 asks for the house of silence (மோன வீடு) beyond the mind, where nothing else is spoken.

Tirumular gives form and formlessness and the thirty-six tattvas to Shakti and Siva; 736 gives the same pairs, form and formless, difference and non-difference, bindu and nada, to Murugan and ends 'the one is you'.

Both ask to be set among the Lord's devotees as the way out of the round of births: 722 asks to be counted in the throng of servants, 738 to have those who think of Murugan as companions so as not to drown in the sea of seven births.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives before any scheme to avert it; 742 cites the same elders' word and grants it (தகவாம் அது), yet asks for the Lord's grace to free him from what fate brings. Not a tension, since the poet does not deny the saying: grace is set beside fate as the one thing no human scheme is.
audit_text_issue: Several lines of 742 are hard to split, as the marker notes.

note: Both are love-sickness songs with the stock torments of moon, Kama's arrows and night or evening, sung to Murugan in a lover's voice rather than as the poet's confession.
audit_text_issue: 739's படியொதான் and the place name திருவர்முர் look corrupt (திருவாமூர்).

note: Both turn the plea into a yogic programme, breath, the sun's path, the sky and the dance in 744; muladhara, the three mandalas, bindu and nada and the central pillar in 762; and both praise Murugan as the saint who sent the Jains to the stake.

Both see the body as a vessel of filth with nine openings; the Naladiyar uses it to mock the man who praises a woman's arms, 745 to confess the poet's own frame and ask, before thought fails, for teaching.
Both confess the poet's trade of praising patrons in verse for gifts, likening men to gods (Vishnu of the milk sea here, clouds in giving in 15), and ask to be turned from it.
15 confesses praising patrons as Tamil's refuge; 749 lists the patrons, fools, misers, gamblers, and the result, the poet ruined and lying in the fire of poverty.
The Kural says nothing is more shameful to the tongue than begging; 749 confesses a tongue spent praising unworthy men and a life left in poverty.
Both picture old age by faltering steps, the staff and fallen teeth; the Naladiyar faults the old man still clinging to desire, 752 asks to be freed from the birth that brings such an end.

Both build the courtesan's arts on the verb of showing (காட்டுவர், காட்டி). 1183 adds robbery and the love-drug; 1176 turns the verb back on Siva and Murugan, asking to be shown the feet instead.

Both describe women who take all the wealth from a man's hands while he believes in their love. The Naladiyar ends in the town's laughter at the fool; 1183 ends in a plea to be taken out of that union.

Both give Murugan the love-sickness the poet confesses: the south wind and Kama's arrows wound him until he goes to Valli in the millet field. 1181 puts in his mouth the plea to save his life from love's fever.
Both are a mother's lament for a daughter lovesick for Murugan, worn by the moon, the wind and the evening; 24 adds the anril bird, 1189 the gossiping women and the herdsman's flute.
The herdsman's flute as a weapon of evening: the Kural's woman calls it a messenger of the burning dusk that kills, and in 1189 the cowherd's flute is among the things wearing the girl down.
audit_text_issue: 1189 has corrupt characters (லு஡தி).

note: The Naladiyar sketches the old man whose speech fails and teeth fall but who still keeps his eyes on desire; 1194 lists every stage of that decay down to the stench of the sickbed and turns it into a plea for grace at the last moment.
Both picture Yama's palm-leaf summons with drums, the bier and wailing kin; 23 draws the lesson of sharing before it comes, 1215 asks instead for love of the anklets.
Both name the courtesan's want as money, not love: the Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth bring harm, and 1214 calls them women whose minds seek coins.

Both follow the corpse from the house: the kin strip him or wrap him in torn cloth, light the pyre and then bathe. The Tirumanthiram calls them people without justice; 1227 calls life itself pure falsehood and asks for the state of Siva.

The Kural's women who weigh the profit before they speak match 1231's women who sell love after reckoning the coins in a man's hand (கைக்காசின் அளவறிந்து); 1231 adds the poets who sing such women's bodies.
audit_text_issue: Encoding glitches in the praise (சுக்஡ணவ, தசக்஡ணவ)

note: Both confess the court poet's sin of singing a patron in borrowed praise for gain; 1226 calls the stock comparisons stolen, 1022 the patron undeserving, and both turn the song to the feet.
Tirumular explains salokam, samipam and sarupam as stages gained through chariyai and the paths after it; 1221 names Murugan lord of the devotees of exactly these three, stopping short of sayujyam.
audit_text_issue: 1221 line 10 garbled (அ ளுறித்) and சர்ருப for சாரூப.

note: Tirumular's dead man leaves the honey-haired woman, the wealth and the house and is carried to the common burning ground; 1235 lists wife, servants, clan and gathered wealth and ends with the body in a small old rag at the burning ground.
audit_text_issue: TM 155 line 4 'மதுவூர வாங்கியே' is obscure; 1235's 'அரிடசுடு' looks garbled.

note: Tirumular's sectarians stay inside their sect and never gain the experience free of ego; 1246 asks whether one should speak endlessly as scripture instead of seeking the one cause known by experience (அநுபூதி), having said 'enough' to the sects.

Tirumular says people wander off calling this or that the supreme and that going the ordained way stills the mind's 'that or this' (அது இது); 1247 asks to know, without quarrelling with the sects, the Lord beyond he, she and it, this and that.
The Naladiyar's wise see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; 1252 calls the poet's own life a bubble (புற்புதப் பிராணன்) and asks for the true word instead.
Both are akam laments at dusk with the south wind, the moon, the anril bird and Kama's arrows; 24 is in a mother's voice, 1254 in the girl's own, asking for the hero's garland.

The Naladiyar's 'he stood, he sat, he lay, and with kin wailing he was gone' urges virtue now; 1265 extends the same list of verbs from birth to corpse (பிறந்தார் கிடந்தார் இருந்தார் தவழ்ந்தார் நடந்தார்) and turns it into a plea for the Lord's 'fear not'.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks where the woman is among them; 1270 calls the body a cage of filth, skin, water and bone, but draws service to the Lord from it rather than disgust at women.
audit_text_issue: 1270's text is largely hard to construe; the marker flagged it.

note: Tirumular rouses the root and joins it to the head through the middle channel to reach the holy feet; 1275 asks for the light above the root centre and the steady gem-light in the middle path.
audit_text_issue: 1275 line 'நநடு ழிதனிலை' is corrupt (doubled syllable, probably நடு வழி).

note: Both set a list of kin against Death's coming: 1266 with Death's rope and a household quarrelling over property, 1267 with Yama on the buffalo and a grief for kin called illusory.
Two vows rather than pleas: 1255 will speak only of the feet whether king or poor, 1276 will not forget them even in the deluded embrace of women.
Both akam laments end with a request for the hero's flowers, his garland in 1254 and kura blossoms in 1268, against Kama's arrows and the sea.
The same four lines of plea, Kama's arrows, the blue sea, the cuckoo of the grove and 'embrace the deer', with only the epithets changed; the two read as variants of one song.
Both songs end by naming Murugan as Sambandar: 1282 by name and by his child's dance, 1287 by the milk of Uma and the impaling of the Jains, and both credit him with filling the land with Tamil.
The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; 1289 dramatizes those words (laughing talk, soothing care) and ends with the plunder of wealth.
Both name 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது) as what must be cut; the Kural promises a world above the gods to whoever cuts them, and 1292 asks the cutting itself as a gift of knowledge.

In both the town's gossip feeds the girl's love-sickness rather than ending it; the Kural makes it manure for the sickness, and 1297 sets the reproach of women beside Kama and the moon as what sinks her in sorrow.
The same frame, the moon, Kama and a question ending -லாமோ, closing on தம்பிரானே; 1290 asks about the girl, 1303 is her own voice and adds the world's reproach.
The Kural opens with A as first of letters and God as first of the world; 1307 makes Murugan the letter A itself (அகரமுமாகி), and the one above the three gods.
Both turn into a catalogue of shrines; 1306 is wholly the list, while 1313 sets the list after a yogic ascent, as if the outer pilgrimage answered the inner one.
audit_text_issue: Both have corrupt glyphs (஧வ்ளுர், நாவலு஡ர், வயலு஡ரா).

note: The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who want wealth, not love, bring harm; 1317 names their lavish lying speech and love set at a price, and adds the brass polished to pass for gold.

The Naladiyar sees the old man with failed speech, a staff and lost teeth still eyeing desire; 1321 gives the same old age in detail, adds the medicines, and draws the remedy not from renunciation but from song and the feet.
Both confess the poet's craft spent for wealth: 1092 the praise-songs sung to patrons who gave nothing, 1323 the arts and poems learned and sung while running the streets after money.

Both mark the end by the physician giving up (Tirumular's lets go the pulse, 1325's says no remedy will work) while wife and wealth stay behind or wail; Tirumular leaves it there, while 1325 asks for Murugan to come at that hour.
